awd_abstract_narration:
This award supports participation in the Southwest Local Algebra Meeting at Arizona State University, which will be held March 1–2, 2025. The research presented at this conference will focus on recent advances across the broad mathematical field of algebra, and on applications of the field. The conference talks will aim to be understandable to the graduate student participants, exposing then to techniques from neighboring mathematical areas. These student participants will also be given the opportunity to present their own results at scheduled poster sessions. The wide range of topics and the event schedule are designed to promote mathematical discussion and collaboration, including among researchers in the southwest and southern United States.

The conference speakers will present research in algebraic and enumerative combinatorics, algebraic geometry, and both commutative and noncommutative algebra.  The speakers are experts in, e.g., the study of singularities in positive characteristic, hyperplane arrangements, combinatorial free resolutions, graded Hecke algebras, and symbolic powers. More information can be found on the conference webpage: https://www.math.ttu.edu/~lchriste/slam2025.html.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The 15th annual Southwest Local Algebra Meeting (SLAM) occurred at Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ, March 1-2, 2025. Junior and senior mathematicians working in algebraic fields from institutions across the Southwest met to share research ideas. 74 participants registered for the meeting, including 27 graduate students and 18 untenured faculty and post-docs.

Previous meetings took place at the UT Arlington in 2010, New Mexico State in 2011, Texas Tech in 2012, the University of Arizona in 2013, Texas A&M in 2014, Oklahoma State in 2015, Texas State in 2016, the University of New Mexico in 2017, the University of Arkansas in 2018, the UT El Paso in 2019, Tulane in 2020, Baylor in 2022, University of North Texas in 2023, and University of Oklahoma in 2024. 

Participants met at Arizona State University for talks on combinatorics, representation theory, and commutative algebra. Anurag Singh (University of Utah) gave the keynote address, with additional talks by Sankhaneel Bisui (Arizona State), Naomi Krawzik (Sam Houston State), Arvind Kumar (New Mexico State), Soho Oh (Texas State), and Elisa Palezzato (Hokkaido University). Participants included 59 mathematicians from Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Indiana, Louisiana, Nebraska, New Mexico, North Carolina, Texas, Oklahoma, Utah,  Brazil and Mexico. NSF funds were used primarily to support travel and lodging for US-based students and faculty with limited local travel support.

There were 18 posters, by 15 graduate students, 2 post-doc, and 1 faculty member. Presenters gave their ideas in discussions with other researchers. The posters were

• Tatheer Ajani (UT Arlington, Self-Tor Persistence of Modules over Determinantal Ideals)

• Raul Alvarez (UT Rio Grande Valley, A DG algebra structure with divided powers on the generalized Taylor resolution)

• Reid Buchanan (Oklahoma State, Macaulay coefficients and decomposing lex segments)

• Hoai Dao (Oklahoma State, Resolutions of pinched power ideals)

• Sudipta Das (Arizona State, Asymptotic colength for families of ideals: an analytic approach)

• Karthik Ganapathy (UC San Diego, Non-noetherianity of GL-algebras in characteristic two)

• Katie Grebel (UT Arlington, Life inside the triangle)

• Haoxi Hu (Tulane, Symbolic powers via extensions)

• Dipendranath Mahato (Tulane, Interpolation of projective points and Demailly's conjecture)

• Victor Daniel Mendoza Rubio (University of Sao Paulo, Certain homological dimensions, and vanishing of Ext and Tor)

• Ritika Nair (Oklahoma State, Vertex decomposability of simplicial complexes with many facets)

• Benjamin Oltsik (University of Connecticut, Symbolic Defect of Monomial Ideals)

• Anh Vinh Pham (Tulane, Newton-nondegenerate ideals in regular local rings)

• Juan Ramirez (Notre Dame, Bidegrees for the defining equations of Rees algebras of some ideals in two variables)

• Richard Sayanagi (New Mexico State, Power series rings over zero-dimensional rings)

• Aniketh Sivakumar (Tulane, Partial Betti splittings with applications to binomial edge ideals)

• Jonathan Toledo (Instituto Tecnologico del Valle de Etla, Rank of adjacency matrix of ring graphs)

• Linoy Utkina (UT Rio Grande Valley, The Herzog–Takayama resolution over a skew polynomial ring)

 

 

Intellectual Merit: The study of rings, fields, and groups is important in many branches of mathematics, e.g., geometry, group representations, number theory, combinatorics, and homotopy theory.

Algebraists in the Southwest study a variety of topics under the umbrella of ring theory. Geographical distances are large, so spontaneous inter-institution interactions rarely occur. SLAM brings together students and faculty from across the region, and includes time to establish new and reinforce ongoing collaborations.

 

 

Broader Impacts: The participants came from many types of institutions, and included researchers at all career stages. There were ~27 graduate students, 8 post-docs, 10 untenured faculty, 10 tenured faculty, and 2 retired faculty.

Many faculty at non-Ph.D.-granting institutions in the Southwest are graduates of local universities. SLAM offered them an opportunity to strengthen contacts. The location and financial support made it possible for them to participate. Researchers who already have national/international collaborations got a chance to learn of advances in the broader area of algebra and connect with colleagues in the region

The small and informal setting offered graduate students a relaxed introduction to professional meetings. The poster sessions in particular were an ice-breaker, conducive to student-faculty interactions. Many students struck up spirited scientific discussions with faculty and students from other institutions, and the meeting was very helpful for students who were on or about to enter the job market.
